source_text: Pater, si possibile est, transeat calix iste a me; verumtamen non sicut ego volo sed sicut tu. Suscipiens naturam carnis humanae omnes proprietates implevit ut non in phantasia carnem habuisse existimaretur sed in veritate. Proprium est omnis hominis fidelis primum nolle pati, maxime usque ad mortem; si autem voluerit Deus, acquiescere etiam contra voluntatem suam.
thought_title: The Father's will over the Son's human will
orientation: Origen is commenting on Jesus' prayer in Gethsemane, explaining how his sorrow and reluctance belong to the true human nature he took on.
pass_a_gloss: Father, if possible [it] is, let pass cup this from me; nevertheless not as I will but as you. Taking up [the] nature of flesh human all [the] properties he fulfilled so that not in phantasy flesh to have had he might be thought but in truth. [The] proper [thing] is of every man faithful first to be unwilling to suffer, especially up to death; if however should will God, to acquiesce even against will his [own].

choices.why: The glossary requires 'cup' for calix, and 'this' preserves the demonstrative force of iste.

choices.english: taking up the nature of human flesh
choices.why: Suscipiens is a participle of means or manner; 'taking up' keeps the active sense of assuming human nature.
rejected: having received the nature of human flesh
assuming the nature of human flesh

choices.why: Phantasia here contrasts with truth, meaning mere seeming or illusion; 'appearance' captures that without importing modern psychological senses.

choices.english: to acquiesce even against one's own will
choices.why: Acquiescere means to yield or consent; 'acquiesce' preserves the sense of yielding to God's will while retaining the tension with one's own will.
rejected: to consent even against his own will
to submit even against his own will

bible_refs.note: Pater, si possibile est, transeat calix iste a me; verumtamen non sicut ego volo sed sicut tu

pass_b_english: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; yet not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26:39). In taking up the nature of human flesh, he fulfilled all its properties, so that he would not be thought to have had flesh in appearance only, but in truth. It is proper to every faithful person first to refuse to suffer, especially to the point of death; but if God wills it, to acquiesce even against one's own will.
